sentences: She visited Parliament House in Canberra and found it both a working building and a civic symbol.
He found the Australian Parliament the most publicly accessible democratic institution he had encountered.
Parliament is the supreme legislative body of a democratic state — in Australia, the federal Parliament.
She found the Australian Parliament comprising two chambers: the Senate and the House of Representatives.
He found the Parliament of Australia sitting in Canberra — the national capital.
Parliament passes laws, holds the government to account, and represents the Australian people.
She found parliament question time the most theatrical and most revealing daily political event.
He found every Australian state and territory also having its own parliament.
Parliament House opened in 1988 — built into the side of Capital Hill in Canberra.
She describes visiting Parliament House as the civics experience that most made democratic process feel tangible.
She found the Senate the upper house — each state sending twelve senators regardless of population.
He found the Senate the most powerful legislative check on government in Australia.
The Senate is the upper house of the Australian Parliament — its role is to review legislation.
She found the Senate's proportional voting system allowing minor parties to win seats.
He found the Senate able to block government legislation — the balance of power frequently held by crossbenchers.
Senators serve six-year terms — half the Senate faces election every three years.
She found the Senate Estimates process the most detailed parliamentary accountability mechanism.
He found the Senate Crossbench — Greens, independents — playing a decisive role in shaping legislation.
The Senate is often called the States' House — it was designed to represent state interests equally.
She describes the Senate as the chamber she most underestimated before understanding its power.
She found the House of Representatives the lower house — government is formed here based on majority.
He found one hundred and fifty-one members elected to the House of Representatives from single-member electorates.
The House of Representatives is the lower house of the Australian Parliament — where government is formed.
She found all money bills originating in the House of Representatives.
He found the Member of Parliament for his electorate the person most directly accountable to his local community.
The House of Representatives uses preferential voting — every vote counts toward the final result.
She found the House sitting for more weeks than the Senate — it is the primary debating chamber.
He found the Government formed by the party or coalition holding a majority in the House.
The House of Representatives chamber is traditionally decorated in green — the Senate in red.
She describes the distinction between the two houses as the knowledge that most clarified how Australian legislation actually became law.
She found compulsory voting the Australian democratic feature that most surprised people from other countries.
He found compulsory voting producing higher turnout and more centrist political outcomes than optional systems.
Compulsory voting is the legal requirement for enrolled citizens to vote in elections.
She found compulsory voting resulting in over ninety-five percent turnout at Australian elections.
He found compulsory voting enforced by fines — around twenty dollars for failure to vote without a valid reason.
Compulsory voting in Australia applies to federal, state, and territory elections.
She found compulsory voting meaning that Australian politicians could not ignore any segment of the electorate.
He found compulsory voting criticised by some as coercive — and defended by others as ensuring democratic legitimacy.
Compulsory voting does not require casting a formal vote — an informal or blank ballot satisfies the obligation.
She describes compulsory voting as the civic institution she most wished her country of origin also practised.
She found preferential voting requiring her to number candidates from most to least preferred.
He found preferential voting one of Australia's most significant contributions to democratic design.
Preferential voting — also called ranked choice voting — allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference.
She found preferential voting ensuring the winner had the support of a majority of voters.
He found preferential voting preventing a split vote from causing an unwanted outcome.
Preferential voting in the House of Representatives is full preferential — every box must be numbered.
She found Senate voting using above-the-line or below-the-line preferential options.
He found preferential voting making votes for minor parties meaningful — preferences flowed to major parties.
Preferential voting in Australia was introduced federally in 1918.
She describes preferential voting as the electoral system she most wished she could explain to international friends in under a minute.
She found the prime minister accountable to parliament — and ultimately to the electorate.
He found Australia's prime ministers changing with notable frequency over the past two decades.
The prime minister is the head of government in Australia — the leader of the party with majority support.
She found the prime minister's office at Parliament House open to public viewing when not in session.
He found the prime minister's powers derived from convention, not explicit constitutional provision.
The prime minister chairs the Cabinet and is the government's primary public face.
She found Australia having six prime ministers in ten years between 2010 and 2019.
He found the prime minister's official residence — The Lodge in Canberra and Kirribilli in Sydney.
The prime minister represents Australia internationally — at the G20, ASEAN, and bilateral summits.
She describes understanding the prime minister's role as the civics knowledge that most clarified why leadership stability mattered.
She found cabinet decisions the most consequential decisions of Australian government.
He found the cabinet meeting in secret — its deliberations not publicly disclosed.
Cabinet is the group of senior ministers who collectively make government decisions.
She found cabinet comprising around twenty ministers — the most senior members of the governing party.
He found cabinet decisions binding on all ministers — collective responsibility the governing principle.
Cabinet meetings occur regularly in Canberra — and occasionally at special locations.
She found the cabinet's composition reflecting both political and demographic considerations.
He found the cabinet room at Parliament House among the most significant spaces in Australian political life.
Cabinet is supported by the Cabinet Secretariat — which coordinates policy across government.
She describes the cabinet as the decision-making body she most wanted to understand — and found most deliberately opaque.
She found her electorate's boundaries on the AEC website — she was in a marginal seat.
He found the electorate the geographic and administrative unit of democratic representation.
An electorate is a defined geographic area represented by one Member of Parliament.
She found the Australian Electoral Commission redrawing electorate boundaries after each Census.
He found marginal electorates — where the margin of victory is small — the focus of campaign resources.
Electorates in Australia vary enormously in size — from inner-city to vast remote seats.
She found Maranoa — the largest electorate by area — covering most of outback Queensland.
He found the electorate office of his local MP useful for help with federal government matters.
Electorate offices assist constituents with Medicare, Centrelink, immigration, and other federal issues.
She describes finding her electorate as the act that most connected her national identity to her local street.
She voted in the referendum on the Voice to Parliament — one of Australia's most significant democratic events.
He found Australia's referendum process among the strictest in the democratic world.
A referendum is a national vote on a proposed constitutional change.
She found the Australian Constitution requiring a double majority — national majority plus majority in four of six states.
He found only eight of forty-four referendums in Australian history succeeding — a high bar.
Referendums in Australia must pass both a national majority vote and a state majority vote.
She found the 1967 referendum including Aboriginal Australians in the Census one of the most successful.
He found the 2023 Voice to Parliament referendum a significant and contested political moment.
Referendums in Australia are conducted by the Australian Electoral Commission on the same platform as elections.
She describes participating in a referendum as the civic act that most directly placed her in Australian history.
She participated in the postal plebiscite on same-sex marriage in 2017.
He found the plebiscite distinct from a referendum — it does not change the Constitution.
A plebiscite is a national popular vote on a question that does not amend the Constitution.
She found the 2017 marriage equality plebiscite conducted by post — a voluntary survey.
He found plebiscites used when government sought public endorsement without constitutional change.
Plebiscites in Australia have been used for conscription, national songs, and marriage equality.
She found the marriage equality plebiscite result — sixty-two percent yes — enabling legislation.
He found the plebiscite debate about whether the question warranted putting to the public — a legitimate critique.
Plebiscites are not binding in the same sense as referendums — Parliament must still legislate.
She describes the marriage equality plebiscite as the vote she cast most personally — and most publicly shared.
She watched question time in the public gallery — the theatre was both compelling and dispiriting.
He found question time the most publicly visible parliamentary proceedings.
Question time is the daily period in parliament when ministers answer questions from other members.
She found question time televised live — a window into parliamentary culture.
He found government questions — Dorothy Dixers — giving ministers opportunities to promote policy.
Question time in the House of Representatives runs for approximately one hour on sitting days.
She found the tone of question time reflecting the political temperature — tense or combative.
He found the speaker presiding over question time and maintaining order — not always successfully.
Question time is distinct from Senate Estimates — which provides more detailed and technical scrutiny.
She describes watching question time as the activity that most calibrated her expectations of political discourse.
She found lobbying the most powerful and least visible form of influence on Australian policy.
He found the lobbyist register publicly available — but not all lobbyists disclosed their clients.
Lobbying is the activity of attempting to influence government decisions on behalf of a group or interest.
She found professional lobbying firms operating primarily in Canberra — close to Parliament House.
He found the lobbying industry representing industry groups, corporations, NGOs, and unions.
Lobbying in Australia requires registration with the Australian Government Lobbyist Register.
She found the revolving door between government and lobbying firms a significant transparency concern.
He found lobbying transparency reform a persistent advocacy cause for civil society organisations.
Lobbying includes meetings with ministers, policy submissions, and media campaigns.
She describes lobbying as the political activity that most required citizens to develop countervailing civic capacity.

words.meaning: çapraz sıra (bağımsız veya küçük parti milletvekilleri)
sentences: She found the crossbench holding the balance of power in the Senate — a position of significant influence.
He found the crossbench comprising Greens senators, independents, and minor party representatives.
The crossbench refers to parliamentarians who belong to neither the government nor the official opposition.
She found crossbench senators negotiating with the government to pass contested legislation.
He found the crossbench growing in influence as Australians voted beyond the major parties.
Crossbench members in the House of Representatives — particularly independents — have increased in recent elections.
She found crossbench positions on climate, integrity, and housing often more progressive than major parties.
He found the crossbench most powerful when neither major party held a Senate majority.
Crossbench bargaining shaped major legislation — climate policy, housing, and tax reform.
She describes the crossbench as the parliamentary grouping she most closely watched to understand where real negotiation happened.
She watched the federal budget announcement — the Medicare and housing measures directly affected her.
He found the federal budget the most consequential annual document in Australian economic policy.
The federal budget is the government's annual statement of revenues, expenditures, and economic forecasts.
She found the federal budget handed down by the Treasurer on the second Tuesday in May.
He found budget night coverage the most watched annual economic television event in Australia.
The federal budget funds defence, health, education, welfare, and infrastructure across Australia.
She found the budget papers running to thousands of pages — the summary the most practical starting point.
He found the budget surplus or deficit the most discussed headline figure in media coverage.
Budget measures can take effect from the following financial year — or sometimes immediately.
She describes reading the federal budget as the annual exercise that most connected government spending to her daily life.
She found the Treasurer responsible for the nation's economic management and budget presentation.
He found the Treasurer the minister whose decisions most directly affected household finances.
The Treasurer is the senior minister responsible for fiscal policy, taxation, and the federal budget.
She found the Treasurer delivering the budget speech — the most significant economic address of the year.
He found the Treasurer appearing regularly on economic and business media — the financial face of government.
The Treasurer works alongside the Reserve Bank but maintains institutional independence from it.
She found notable Treasurers — Paul Keating, Peter Costello — shaping decades of Australian economic direction.
He found the Treasurer responsible for the MYEFO — Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook — update.
The Treasurer chairs the Expenditure Review Committee — scrutinising budget proposals from all ministers.
She describes the Treasurer's role as the ministerial position she most directly felt the effect of in her working life.
She contacted the local council about the footpath damage outside her house.
He found the local council the most accessible tier of Australian government.
A local council is the elected body responsible for local government within a municipality.
She found local councils responsible for roads, footpaths, parks, libraries, and waste collection.
He found local council elections held every four years in most states.
Local councils in Australia number over five hundred — ranging from small rural to large metropolitan.
She found the council website her first stop for planning permits, bin day calendars, and local events.
He found local council rates the primary funding mechanism for local government services.
Local councils set and enforce planning regulations within their boundaries.
She describes the local council as the level of government she most directly experienced in her daily life.
She complained to the Commonwealth Ombudsman after the agency failed to respond for six months.
He found the Ombudsman an independent reviewer of government agency conduct.
An ombudsman is an independent officer investigating complaints about government agencies or businesses.
She found the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman handling complaints about phone and internet providers.
He found the Financial Services Ombudsman — now AFCA — resolving complaints about banks and insurers.
Ombudsman offices are free to complainants — the service is government or industry funded.
She found the ombudsman process informal — no legal representation required.
He found the ombudsman having the power to recommend remedies — but not always to enforce them.
Australia has multiple ombudsmen — Commonwealth, state, and industry-specific.
She describes contacting the Ombudsman as the step that most reliably moved a stalled complaint forward.
She found Australia's human rights framework a patchwork — no single federal bill of rights.
He found the Australian Human Rights Commission the primary federal institution for human rights protection.
Human rights are the fundamental rights and freedoms to which all people are entitled.
She found Australia's human rights protections inconsistent — strong in some areas, weak in others.
He found Victoria and the ACT having dedicated Human Rights Acts — unlike most other states.
Human rights in Australia are protected through legislation, common law, and international obligations.
She found the debate about a federal Human Rights Act recurring in Australian political discourse.
He found international human rights obligations — the ICCPR and ICESCR — binding on Australia.
Human rights monitoring in Australia includes the AHRC's annual review of the government's record.
She describes advocating for human rights as the civic work she most wanted her professional skills to contribute to.
She found judicial review the mechanism by which courts assessed whether government action was lawful.
He found the Administrative Appeals Tribunal providing review of government decisions.
Judicial review is the power of courts to examine and potentially invalidate government decisions.
She found judicial review available for administrative decisions — visa refusals, benefit denials, and licensing.
He found the Federal Court and the High Court exercising the most significant judicial review powers.
Judicial review does not allow courts to substitute their judgment — it examines legality, not merits.
She found judicial review outcomes including setting aside decisions, remitting matters, and declaratory relief.
He found merit review — through the AAT — distinct from judicial review.
Judicial review has shaped Australian administrative law — protecting citizens from unlawful government action.
She describes understanding judicial review as the legal knowledge that most gave her confidence in the rule of law.
She followed the High Court's constitutional decision — it reshaped the boundaries of federal power.
He found the High Court of Australia the most powerful legal institution in the country.
The High Court of Australia is the nation's apex court — with final jurisdiction on constitutional matters.
She found the High Court comprising seven justices — appointed by the federal government.
He found the High Court's decisions binding on all other Australian courts.
The High Court sits in Canberra primarily, with hearings also conducted in state capitals.
She found landmark High Court decisions — Mabo, Wik — shaping Native Title law.
He found the High Court exercising original jurisdiction in some matters — not only appeals.
The High Court interprets the Australian Constitution — its decisions are the final word.
She describes the High Court as the institution she most turned to understand what Australian law actually permitted.
She enrolled to vote through the AEC website — the process took less than five minutes.
He found the AEC the most trusted federal government agency in public surveys.
The Australian Electoral Commission — AEC — administers federal elections, referendums, and electoral roll.
She found the AEC responsible for electoral enrolment, polling, and result declaration.
He found the AEC maintaining the electoral roll — he updated his address after moving.
The AEC is an independent statutory authority — free from political direction.
She found the AEC providing a polling booth locator — she found her local booth within seconds.
He found the AEC also overseeing party registration and the disclosure of political donations.
The AEC provides educational resources about voting — she used them when explaining preferential voting.
She describes the AEC as the institution she most relied on to believe the election was being conducted honestly.
She found political donation disclosures published annually — below the threshold of fifteen thousand dollars, nothing was required.
He found the donation disclosure threshold a persistent reform issue — critics wanting lower limits.
Donation disclosure is the legal obligation to report political donations above a threshold.
She found federal disclosure reporting happening annually — with a significant lag in public information.
He found the donor, amount, and recipient published on the AEC website.
Donation disclosure in Australia applies to donations to political parties, candidates, and associated entities.
She found real-time disclosure advocated by transparency groups — the current annual system was slow.
He found foreign donations banned — Australian law prohibiting overseas political contributions.
Donation disclosure enables public scrutiny of the financial relationships shaping political parties.
She describes reading the donation disclosures as the political transparency exercise that most disappointed and clarified simultaneously.
She found the National Anti-Corruption Commission established after significant public pressure.
He found integrity commissions operating at state level for years before the federal equivalent.
An integrity commission investigates corruption, misconduct, and serious integrity breaches in public office.
She found NACC — the National Anti-Corruption Commission — beginning operations in 2023.
He found state integrity commissions — ICAC in NSW, IBAC in Victoria — with significant investigative track records.
Integrity commissions investigate public officials, parliamentarians, and their staff.
She found integrity commission hearings sometimes public — the evidence ventilated before an audience.
He found the integrity commission's findings not always resulting in criminal prosecution — but often in resignation.
Integrity commissions are independent — they cannot be directed by the government they scrutinise.
She describes the establishment of an integrity commission as the accountability reform she most hoped would change behaviour.
She lodged a freedom of information request for the ministerial briefing — she received it six weeks later.
He found freedom of information requests a powerful tool for investigative journalism.
Freedom of information — FOI — is the right to access documents held by government agencies.
She found the FOI Act 1982 governing federal government document access in Australia.
He found FOI requests submitted through the relevant agency — most now via online portals.
Freedom of information can be refused on grounds including national security, legal privilege, and cabinet confidentiality.
She found FOI requests taking thirty days — or longer with extensions — to be processed.
He found the Information Commissioner reviewing FOI refusals when applicants believed the refusal was wrong.
Freedom of information enables citizens, journalists, and researchers to hold government to account.
She describes the FOI request as the accountability tool she most wished she had used earlier in her advocacy.
She visited Canberra for the first time and found it a more interesting city than her preconceptions had suggested.
He found Canberra the most deliberately designed city in Australia — built for the purpose of governance.
Canberra is the capital city of Australia — home to the federal parliament and national institutions.
She found Canberra chosen as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne in 1908.
He found Canberra's planned design by Walter Burley Griffin giving it a lake and radial boulevard structure.
Canberra houses the Parliament, High Court, National Gallery, National Museum, and War Memorial.
She found Canberra smaller than expected but richer in cultural institutions than any comparable city.
He found Canberra's public service culture shaping the national policy conversation.
Canberra is in the Australian Capital Territory — a self-governing territory separate from New South Wales.
She describes Canberra as the Australian city she most undervalued — and most revised her opinion of after visiting.
She watched Senate Estimates online — officials were asked detailed and uncomfortable questions.
He found Senate Estimates the most detailed and sustained parliamentary accountability process.
Senate Estimates is the process by which Senate committees scrutinise government agency expenditure.
She found Senate Estimates running for days — covering every department and agency.
He found Senate Estimates the venue for the most technically sophisticated questioning in Australian politics.
Senate Estimates allows senators to question public servants directly — ministers may also appear.
She found Senate Estimates hearings available on the APH website — fully searchable and archived.
He found Senate Estimates revelations regularly generating significant media coverage.
Estimates committees divide the Senate's portfolio responsibilities — each covering specific agencies.
She describes Senate Estimates as the accountability mechanism she most wished more Australians watched.
She found the Australian Constitution the foundational legal document establishing the Commonwealth.
He found the Constitution remarkably brief — one hundred and twenty-eight sections.
The Constitution is Australia's founding legal document — establishing the powers and structure of government.
She found the Constitution adopted in 1901 — at Federation.
He found the Constitution difficult to amend — requiring a double majority referendum.
The Constitution distributes powers between federal and state governments.
She found Constitutional interpretation by the High Court the most significant ongoing legal process in Australia.
He found the Constitution surprisingly readable — though the interpretive case law was dense.
The Australian Constitution does not contain an explicit bill of rights — a long-debated omission.
She describes the Constitution as the document she most wished had been explained to her at the beginning of citizenship.
She found Federation the founding moment of the Australian nation — 1 January 1901.
He found the story of Federation involving decades of negotiation between the colonies.
Federation is the process by which Australia's six colonies united to form the Commonwealth of Australia.
She found Federation creating the federal structure — dividing powers between the new Commonwealth and the states.
He found the Federation Convention debates the most sophisticated political deliberation in Australian history.
Federation in 1901 was a political and constitutional achievement — not independence from Britain.
She found the first Federal Parliament opening in Melbourne — Canberra was not yet built.
He found the Constitution drafted at Federation conventions — drawing on British, Canadian, and American models.
Federation left some matters — most critically the rights of Aboriginal people — shamefully unresolved.
She describes learning about Federation as the history that most changed how she understood the Australia she lived in.
She found the separation of powers the constitutional principle most protecting Australian democracy.
He found the separation between executive, legislative, and judicial power the structural guarantee of freedom.
The separation of powers divides government authority among the legislature, executive, and judiciary.
She found Australia's separation of powers partially Westminster — the executive sits within the legislature.
He found the judiciary's independence from the executive the most critical element of the separation.
The separation of powers prevents the concentration of authority — each branch checking the others.
She found the High Court's enforcement of constitutional boundaries the most significant practical expression of separation of powers.
He found debates about executive overreach during the COVID period testing the separation of powers.
The separation of powers is not perfectly realised in any system — but the principle shapes the architecture.
She describes the separation of powers as the constitutional design she most appreciated the more she understood it.
She made the citizenship pledge at the ceremony — she meant every word of it.
He found the citizenship pledge the formal commitment that completed the naturalisation process.
The citizenship pledge is the statement made at a citizenship ceremony committing to Australia and its values.
She found the pledge committing her to sharing Australian values, obeying the laws, and fulfilling civic duties.
He found the full pledge including both a secular and a religious version — she chose the secular form.
The citizenship pledge is made publicly — family and community as witnesses.
She found the pledge's language simple but meaningful — it named the commitment she had already made in her life.
He found the pledge read together by all new citizens simultaneously — the collective moment was powerful.
The citizenship pledge replaced the Oath of Allegiance in 1994 — it now speaks of shared values.
She describes making the citizenship pledge as the public moment she most had wanted to reach — and found completely worthy of it.
She searched Hansard for the minister's exact words — she found a sentence that contradicted the current position.
He found Hansard the most authoritative record of what was said in Australian parliament.
Hansard is the official verbatim record of parliamentary debates and proceedings.
She found Hansard publicly searchable at aph.gov.au — every word spoken in parliament since 1901.
He found Hansard used by journalists, researchers, lawyers, and citizens seeking the parliamentary record.
Hansard is published after each sitting day — sometimes with minor corrections.
She found Hansard the most reliable source for checking what a politician had actually promised.
He found Hansard named after Luke Hansard — the English printer who first published parliamentary debates.
Hansard records both chambers — House of Representatives and Senate — as well as committee hearings.
She describes searching Hansard as the research habit that most consistently found what she was looking for in the public record.

sentences: She lived in a marginal seat — campaign visits from party leaders were a regular inconvenience.
He found marginal seats the most intensively contested areas at every Australian election.
A marginal seat is an electorate where the incumbent's winning margin is small — typically less than six percent.
She found election campaigns concentrated resources on marginal seats — safe seats were largely ignored.
He found the swing required to change a marginal seat calculated precisely by electoral analysts.
Marginal seats determine government — parties target them with candidate selection, advertising, and announcements.
She found living in a marginal seat meaning every party came to her door.
He found marginal seats in outer suburban Australia often decisive in federal elections.
Marginal seat analysis is the core of campaign strategy — swing voters in these seats determined the outcome.
She describes living in a marginal seat as the electoral experience that most made her feel her vote had specific, visible weight.

words.meaning: sırasına göre oy (gerçek seçim tercihi olmaksızın)
sentences: She found the donkey vote benefiting the candidate listed first on the ballot paper.
He found the AEC randomising ballot order in some elections to reduce the donkey vote effect.
A donkey vote is a ballot completed by numbering boxes sequentially from top to bottom without genuine preference.
She found donkey voting estimated to affect one to three percent of votes — sometimes decisive in close contests.
He found donkey votes formal — they counted toward results, unlike informal ballots.
Donkey voting favours the first-listed candidate — candidate order matters in close elections.
She found the randomised ballot order in Senate elections designed to equalise the donkey vote effect.
He found compulsory voting increasing the donkey vote — some voters satisfied the obligation without choosing.
Donkey votes are distinguished from informal votes — informal ballots are not counted at all.
She describes the donkey vote as the voting behaviour that most demonstrated the gap between obligation and civic engagement.
She found the polling booth at the local primary school — open from eight in the morning.
He found the sausage sizzle at the polling booth the most beloved Australian electoral tradition.
A polling booth is a venue where voters cast their ballots on election day.
She found polling booths in schools, town halls, and community centres across the electorate.
He found early voting centres operating for two weeks before election day.
Polling booths in Australia are managed by AEC officials — security and neutrality maintained.
She found the polling booth process quick — the queue moved at a predictable pace.
He found absent voting available at any polling booth — not required to vote in home electorate.
Polling booths open at eight in the morning and close at six in the evening on election day.
She describes arriving at the polling booth as the civic ritual she most looked forward to every three years.
She found the caretaker period between the election call and the result a time of constrained government action.
He found the caretaker conventions limiting what the incumbent government could announce or commit to.
A caretaker government is the incumbent government during a federal election campaign — operating under restricted conventions.
She found caretaker conventions preventing major policy announcements, significant appointments, and international commitments.
He found the caretaker period typically running from the election writ being issued to the new government's formation.
Caretaker governments can respond to emergencies — the restrictions concern discretionary decisions.
She found the caretaker period lasting five to six weeks in Australian federal elections.
He found the concept of caretaker government protecting democratic neutrality during campaigns.
Caretaker conventions are not legally binding but are observed as an important constitutional convention.
She describes the caretaker period as the democratic moment that most clearly showed the difference between governing and campaigning.
